blocks.text: When computer mapping began in New Zealand government offices, the map was already there. Survey plans, cadastral record maps, trig observations, coordinate lists, aerial photographs, census boundaries, topographic sheets, hydrographic charts and resource maps had been made for different jobs by different agencies. The first computer users inherited separate records with their own scales, identifiers and maintenance routines.

Survey plans, cadastral record maps, trig observations, coordinate lists, aerial photographs, census boundaries, topographic sheets, hydrographic charts and resource maps had been made for different jobs by different agencies. The first computer users inherited separate records with their own scales, identifiers and maintenance routines.

blocks.text: Those records were not neutral snapshots. Cadastral maps represented title and land administration, including the Crown’s recording of Māori land. Census maps divided people into areas chosen for counting. Topographic sheets selected and generalised features for a particular scale. Place names reflected official spelling and naming decisions. Digitising made these records easier to copy and compare; it did not change how, why or by whom the original lines had been drawn.

blocks.text: Paper records stayed useful because staff kept them current: adding subdivisions to cadastral sheets, replacing old topographic editions, revising enumeration boundaries, indexing aerial film and recalculating survey control. GIS practitioners still recognise the same maintenance work behind a digital layer.

blocks.text: In 1793, Tuki Te Terenui Whare Pirau and Huru were kidnapped from near the Cavalli Islands and taken to Norfolk Island. There, Tuki drew a map for Governor Philip Gidley King. It conveyed geographic knowledge through named places, routes and relationships; it was not a survey plan to be read for scale or bearings. The National Library’s explanatory account spells his companion’s name Huru, while its map catalogue uses Huku. This chapter preserves both spellings rather than infer a fuller identity.

blocks.text: In 1856 at Tūtūrau, Reko explained the South Island interior to surveyor John Turnbull Thomson and drew a map in dust. Thomson later carried out reconnaissance and published maps of the region. The records connect that work with Reko’s knowledge, but they do not establish that any specific published map was copied directly from his drawing.
